newsitem.title: UK: Greenpeace sees environment threat from gene crops.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace sees environment threat from gene crops.

text.p: Genetically modified crops pose a threat to the environment which goes beyond direct human health concerns, a Greenpeace official said on Tuesday.
"Greenpeace's opposition to genetic modification is not just because of potential food allergies or unexpected side-effects," said Douglas Par.
"We also believe growing these crops pose environmental risks," he said.
There was a danger that genetically modified material could be transferred from one species to another, creating a form of "genetic pollution."

According to Parr, the development of a genetically modified tomato now widely on sale in processed form in the UK had shown how difficult it was to predict the effects of altering the genetic make-up of a plant.
Changes designed to slow the softening process in the tomatoes had also reduced the water content and made the tomatoes more resistant to some kinds of fungus, he said.
"You're dealing with systems," he said. "We don't really understand how that works."
He named a series of conceivable side effects such as the plant becoming an invasive weed, interbreeding with new species or the modified gene being exchanged with soil bacteria.
There were similar concerns where human health was being examined directly.

A spokesman for the UK Department of the Environment said that the main worry was that an antibiotic resistant gene could be transferred to animals and so could find its way into the human digestive system.
There was a possibility that certain bacteria in humans would then not respond to antibiotics.
"It won't happen overnight. The bacteria would take time to take over the antibiotic blue print, " he said.

This was the basis of the UK's original rejection of plans to import the maize, he said. But the UK recognised that the risk might be non-existent, or tiny enough to be acceptable, which was why the UK was planning to go along with the decision of EU scientists.

The spokesman said that the UK authorities could see good reasons for being prepared to allow the sale of some genetically modified products. Swiss chemicals company Ciba Geigy AG's maize would avoid the use of pesticides, which would avoid killing other organisms.

"In a world which does have food shortages, anything which increases yields without creating unacceptable risks has to be good. But the authorities have to make sure that there is no risk or that the risk is tiny," he said.
Even if the EU were to decide that there was a problem with the maize, only the unprocessed form would be affected, he said.
According to one of the UK animal feed trade lobby's leaders this meant the likely impact on the trade would be minimal.
Jim Reed, director of the United Kingdom Agricultural Supply Trade Association, told Reuters, "No whole U.S. maize for animal feed is imported directly into the UK."
"A bit gets over from the (European) Continent," he said. "But the likely impact is minimal. Corngluten feed, which is much more widely used in the UK, is not affected."
The EU Commission is due to decide on December 18 whether to allow imports of the modified maize.
